title: Why 93% of Fund Managers Lose to a Simple Index Fund
description:
Over the 20 years to June 2026, more than 9 in 10 actively managed large-cap US stock funds trailed the S&P 500. Why do full-time professionals keep losing to a fund that does no research at all? We explain what an index fund is, William Sharpe's "arithmetic of active management", how a fee gap of less than 1% a year compounds over 30 years, why past winners rarely stay winners, the story of the first index fund (1976) and Warren Buffett's 10-year bet against hedge funds, and the honest weaknesses of index funds: they buy overpriced stocks too, the S&P 500 is top-heavy, and you take the full market crash.

The 30-year fee example is a hypothetical illustration ($100,000, 7% a year before fees, 2025 average asset-weighted expense ratios from ICI), not a prediction. This video explains how markets work; it does not recommend any fund or security.

fr.title: Pourquoi 93 % des gérants perdent face à un fonds indiciel

scenes.say: Over the last twenty years, more than nine out of ten actively managed large US stock funds did worse than one simple benchmark: the S and P five hundred.

visual.label: of large-cap US funds trailed the S&P 500
visual.sub: 20 years to June 2026 · S&P SPIVA scorecard

scenes.say: And it isn't ancient history. In 2025 alone, seventy-nine percent of them fell behind.

visual.title: Large-cap US funds that trailed the S&P 500
visual.note: Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, SPIVA U.S. Scorecards

scenes.say: These are full-time professionals with research teams and huge budgets. And they lost to a fund that does no research at all.
In this video, we'll see why that happens, why it isn't just bad luck, and where index funds have real weaknesses too.
First, what is an index fund?
An index is just a list. The S and P five hundred, for example, is a list of about five hundred of the largest companies in the United States.

visual.label: large US companies, one list: the S&P 500

scenes.say: An index fund simply buys every company on that list, in the same proportions, and holds them. Nobody inside the fund is trying to guess which stocks will win.

visual.title: An index fund, in one line

scenes.say: So who decides what's on the list? For the S and P five hundred, it's a committee at S and P Dow Jones Indices, following published rules about size, profits, and how easily the shares trade.

visual.title: Who picks the S&P 500?
items: A committee at S&P Dow Jones Indices

scenes.say: Bigger companies get a bigger slice of the fund. That's called market cap weighting, and we'll come back to why it matters.

There are index funds for almost everything: the whole US market, stocks around the world, even bonds. In this video we'll mostly use the S and P five hundred, because that's where the best long-term data is.

visual.title: Index funds can track almost any list

scenes.say: And index funds are no longer a niche idea. By the end of 2025, index funds held fifty-two percent of the money in long-term US funds, up from just nineteen percent in 2010.

visual.title: Index funds' share of US long-term fund assets
visual.note: Index mutual funds + index ETFs · Source: ICI 2026 Fact Book

scenes.say: Now, the other side.
An active fund manager tries to beat the index. They research companies, buy the ones they like, skip the ones they don't, and keep trading as their views change.

visual.title: What an active manager does
visual.label: Research, pick stocks, trade, review
visual.sub: the goal: do better than the index

scenes.say: All that research and trading costs money, so active funds charge a higher yearly fee. It's called the expense ratio.

lines.text: whether the fund wins or not

scenes.say: In 2025, the average actively managed stock mutual fund charged zero point six four percent a year. The average index stock mutual fund charged just zero point zero five percent.

visual.title: Average yearly fee, US stock mutual funds (2025)

scenes.say: On ten thousand dollars, that's sixty-four dollars a year versus five dollars. Small numbers. But they repeat every single year.
That means a manager has to beat the market by more than their fee, just to tie with the index fund. So, can they?

visual.text:
To win, a manager must
beat the market by more
than their own fee.
visual.source: The hurdle every active fund faces

scenes.say: Why most of them lose.
In 1991, Nobel prize-winning economist William Sharpe published a short paper called The Arithmetic of Active Management. Its logic is so simple, it's almost annoying.
Think of every dollar invested in the stock market. Some of it sits in index funds. The rest is managed actively. Together, they are the market.
Say the market returns eight percent in a year. Index investors get eight percent. So the average active dollar must also earn eight percent, before costs.
That makes active investing a zero-sum game before costs. For every dollar that beats the market by a point, another dollar trails it by a point.
But then the costs come out. Take away the average fee, and the average active dollar must earn less than the market. Not because managers are foolish. It's just arithmetic.
And fees aren't the only cost. Active funds trade more, so they pay more trading costs. And in a regular taxable account, frequent selling can mean paying tax on gains sooner.

visual.title: Costs that quietly eat returns
visual.label: Yearly fees, trading costs, taxes on gains from selling

scenes.say: Now watch what a small fee does over a long time. Imagine one hundred thousand dollars growing for thirty years, at seven percent a year before fees. This is an illustration, not a prediction.

visual.title: Index fee vs active fee: $100,000 over 30 years

scenes.say: With the average index fee, you'd end up with about seven hundred and fifty thousand dollars. With the average active fee, about six hundred and thirty-six thousand.
That's a gap of almost one hundred and fifteen thousand dollars, from a fee difference of less than one percent a year.
Can't you just pick the winners?
It's the obvious idea: find a fund that's been beating the market, and invest with it. S and P actually tests this, in a report called the Persistence Scorecard.

visual.title: The obvious plan
visual.label: Find a recent winner, invest with it

scenes.say: They took the large US stock funds that ranked in the top quarter of their peers in 2021. There were one hundred and sixty-four of them.

visual.label: large-cap funds in the top quarter in 2021

scenes.say: How many stayed in the top quarter every year through 2025? Zero. Not one.

visual.label: stayed in the top quarter every year to 2025

scenes.say: Even just staying in the top half every year was too much. Only about four and a half percent of funds did it. Pure coin flips would give you six point two five percent.
A big reason is luck. In any single year, plenty of managers will beat the market partly by chance, and chance doesn't repeat on command.
Funds also quietly disappear. Of the large US stock funds that existed twenty years ago, just over a third were still around by mid-2026. The rest were closed or merged away.

visual.title: Large-cap US funds alive in 2006…
visual.note: Source: S&P SPIVA U.S. Scorecard, mid-year 2026

scenes.say: So past winners rarely stay winners. Picking a fund by its recent record is a lot closer to luck than it looks.
Two people made this idea famous.
In 1975, John Bogle founded Vanguard. On August thirty-first, 1976, it launched the first index fund for everyday investors, built to track the S and P five hundred.

visual.title: How the index fund grew up

events.text:
First index fund
for everyday investors

Index funds hold
most fund assets

scenes.say: At first, it flopped. The goal was to raise one hundred and fifty million dollars. It raised just eleven point three million.
But the idea grew into an industry. By the end of 2025, US index mutual funds and ETFs held nineteen point one trillion dollars.

visual.label: in US index mutual funds and ETFs

scenes.say: Then came Warren Buffett. In 2007, he made a one million dollar bet, for charity, that a plain S and P five hundred index fund would beat hedge fund experts over the next ten years.

visual.title: Buffett's bet
visual.label: for charity, 10 years: 2008 to 2017
visual.sub: one S&P 500 index fund vs hedge fund experts

scenes.say: His opponent, Protégé Partners, picked five funds of funds. Together, they owned stakes in more than two hundred hedge funds, and they could switch managers whenever they liked.

visual.title: The other side of the bet

scenes.say: And those funds were expensive. Buffett estimated fixed fees of around two and a half percent of assets every year, before any share of the profits.

visual.label: yearly fixed fees, Buffett's estimate
visual.sub: plus a share of any gains

scenes.say: After ten years, here's the result. The index fund gained one hundred and twenty-five point eight percent. The five funds of funds gained between two point eight and eighty-seven point seven percent.
Per year, the index fund made eight point five percent. The best of the five made six point five, and their average was about three.
The prize had grown to over two point two million dollars, and it went to Girls Inc. of Omaha.

visual.label: donated to Girls Inc. of Omaha

scenes.say: Buffett summed it up in his letter that year: performance comes, performance goes. Fees never falter.

visual.text:
Performance comes,
performance goes.
Fees never falter.

scenes.say: Now, index funds aren't perfect. Here's the honest catch.
First, an index fund holds everything on the list, including companies that may be overpriced. It never asks whether a stock is a bargain. It just buys it.

visual.title: No judgment, by design
visual.label: It buys the bargains… and the overpriced stocks

scenes.say: Second, because bigger companies get bigger slices, the S and P five hundred has become top-heavy. At the end of 2025, its ten largest companies made up about forty-one percent of the whole index.

visual.title: Weight inside the S&P 500, end of 2025

scenes.say: Between 1990 and 2015, that figure mostly sat around eighteen to twenty-three percent. So today, a lot of an S and P five hundred investor's money rides on just a few giant companies.

visual.title: Weight of the 10 largest S&P 500 companies

scenes.say: Third, you get the whole market, including the crashes. In 2008, the index fund in Buffett's bet lost thirty-seven percent. No manager steps in to protect you.
And fourth, an index fund will never beat the market. By design, you get the market's return, minus a small fee.
Some active managers do beat the index, and a few do it for years. The hard part is spotting them before the results are in, not after.

visual.title: Winners do exist
visual.sub: finding them in advance is the hard part

scenes.say: So what does this mean for you?
This isn't advice to buy any particular fund. It's about the principles the evidence points to.
One: costs matter. Every dollar paid in fees is a dollar that stops compounding for you. Check the expense ratio of anything you own.

visual.title: 1 · Costs matter
visual.label: check the expense ratio
visual.sub: average active vs average index fee, 2025

scenes.say: Two: diversify. Owning a broad slice of the market means no single company can sink you, though a top-heavy index is less spread out than it looks.

left.label: One stock
left.sub: one bad year can sink you

scenes.say: Three: think long term. In twenty twenty-five alone, about four in five large-cap funds trailed the S and P five hundred. Over twenty years, more than nine in ten did.

visual.title: 3 · Large-cap funds that trailed the S&P 500
visual.note: Periods ending June 30, 2026 · Source: S&P SPIVA U.S. Scorecard

scenes.say: And four: boring is often smart. Most of investing well is avoiding big, quiet costs, and letting time do the heavy lifting.
Here's the whole video in one line. Most professionals don't lose because they're bad at their jobs. They lose because the math of costs is working against them.

visual.text:
They don't lose
because they're bad.
The math is against them.

scenes.say: If this made markets make a bit more sense, subscribe. We explain how money really works, every week.
